q: According to industry studies on remote access, how do most organizations feel about their ability to secure it?
opts: Confident and satisfied with their current controls
Unhappy with their ability to secure remote access
Indifferent, since remote access is a low priority
Unaware that remote access poses any risk
why: Surveys of security and IT leaders consistently find that most organizations are dissatisfied with how well they can secure remote access for employees and third parties. That dissatisfaction is the business driver behind purpose-built remote access products rather than continuing to stretch VPNs to cover a use case they were never designed for.
wrong: Confidence, indifference and unawareness all describe the opposite of what the research shows — dissatisfaction is the consistent finding, which is why vendors invest in Zero Trust alternatives.

q: Why are organizations' poor confidence scores around securing remote access unsurprising?
opts: Because most remote access is delivered over VPNs, which extend a baseline of network trust to whoever is on the other end
Because remote users never use encryption
Because firewalls block all remote connections by default
Because organizations rarely allow remote access at all
why: Most remote access still runs over VPN, and a VPN's job is to extend the corporate network to the remote endpoint — it authenticates the tunnel, not the ongoing trustworthiness of the user or device. That inherent, coarse-grained trust is exactly what makes organizations uneasy.
wrong: Remote sessions over a VPN are encrypted, so lack of encryption is not the issue. Firewalls do not block sanctioned remote access, and remote access is now the norm, not the exception, which is what makes the trust problem so widespread.

q: What is the core security risk of granting remote access through a traditional VPN?
opts: If an attacker compromises the remote user's machine, the VPN tunnel can give them a path into the corporate network
VPNs cannot encrypt traffic over the public internet
VPN software cannot be centrally patched
VPN concentrators are always placed outside the firewall
why: A VPN authenticates the connection, then largely trusts whatever comes down it. If the endpoint at the other end is compromised, the attacker inherits the same network-level reach the legitimate user had — turning one compromised laptop into a foothold on the internal network.
wrong: VPNs do encrypt the tunnel itself, patching is an operational matter unrelated to the core risk, and concentrator placement varies by design — none of these is the reason VPN-based remote access is considered risky.

q: Which basic privileged access capabilities do traditional VPNs typically fail to provide? (Choose three)
opts: Multi-factor authentication
Automatic password rotation and uniqueness
Session recording and monitoring
An encrypted tunnel for network traffic
why: A VPN's job stops at establishing an encrypted, authenticated tunnel to the network. It has no concept of privileged credentials, so it does not enforce MFA on top of the tunnel, rotate or enforce uniqueness on passwords used behind it, or record and monitor what happens in the resulting session.
wrong: An encrypted tunnel is exactly what a VPN does provide — it is the one item on this list that is core VPN functionality rather than a gap.

q: Why is relying on VPNs or installed agents to secure third-party vendor access particularly problematic for IT teams?
opts: Vendors are legally barred from using VPNs
It requires deploying and managing software on laptops the organization does not own or control, creating ongoing overhead
VPN licenses cannot be issued to non-employees
Vendors are always located outside the VPN's supported regions
why: Vendor and contractor machines belong to another company. Pushing a VPN client or agent onto that hardware means the customer's IT team is now responsible for installing, updating, troubleshooting and eventually removing software on a device it doesn't manage — multiplied across every vendor relationship.
wrong: There is no legal bar on vendors using VPNs, licensing is not the obstacle, and VPN products are not restricted by vendor geography — the real problem is the operational burden of managing software on someone else's endpoint.

q: Why do conventional identity management schemes — provisioning a directory account per person — work poorly for third-party vendors?
opts: Vendors refuse to be issued any kind of account
Vendor access requirements are transient and change frequently, so static, long-lived accounts don't match the real engagement lifecycle
Directory services cannot technically host external accounts
Vendors are only ever given read-only access
why: Vendor engagements start and stop, staff rotate, and the scope of access needed shifts project to project. Standing directory accounts assume a stable population of users, which is the opposite of how third-party relationships actually behave — leaving orphaned accounts and manual cleanup as the norm.
wrong: Vendors can and do accept accounts, directory services happily host external identities, and access level is a policy choice, not a technical limitation — the mismatch is specifically about churn and change frequency.

q: What is CyberArk Remote Access designed to provide?
opts: Fast, easy and secure privileged access for remote vendors and employees, without a VPN
Unrestricted access to all systems for any authenticated user
A replacement for the CyberArk Vault
A hardware appliance for on-premises network segmentation
why: Remote Access is purpose-built to give both remote employees and third-party vendors fast, easy, secure privileged access — closing the gap that VPNs and standing directory accounts leave open, without adding an agent, a VPN client or a vendor-managed password.
wrong: It does not grant unrestricted access — access remains scoped by Safe permissions and Zero Trust checks. It works alongside the Vault and PAM rather than replacing them, and it is a SaaS service, not a hardware appliance.

q: How does CyberArk Remote Access confirm that a connecting user is who they claim to be?
opts: A shared password checked against the target system
The smartphone's biometric capabilities (fingerprint or facial recognition) combined with a dynamic, one-time QR code scanned in the CyberArk Mobile App
A hardware token generating a six-digit code
A static security question answered at logon
why: Identity is proven two ways at once: something the user is (biometric — fingerprint or face, verified locally on the phone) and something tied to that specific login attempt (a short-lived, single-use QR code). Together they replace passwords entirely for the authentication step.
wrong: There is no shared password or security question in this model — that is precisely what the design eliminates. Hardware OTP tokens are a different, older MFA pattern that Remote Access does not rely on.
ref: Remote Access / biometric plus QR authentication

q: What distinguishes CyberArk Remote Access from conventional agent-based remote access solutions?
opts: It is a SaaS-based service built on Zero Trust principles, combined with biometric authentication, rather than an installed agent granting network-level trust
It requires a heavier client agent than competing products
It only supports Windows targets
It relies on a shared organizational password vault presented to end users
why: Remote Access is delivered as a cloud (SaaS) service and applies Zero Trust — verify explicitly, grant least privilege, assume breach — instead of the implicit, network-level trust an agent or VPN client grants once installed. Biometric authentication then anchors identity to a real person rather than a device credential.
wrong: It specifically avoids installing a heavyweight agent, it is not limited to Windows targets, and there is no shared password vault presented to end users — access is brokered without vendors ever handling a target credential.

q: How does CyberArk Remote Access solve the identity-management problem created by constantly changing vendor access needs?
opts: By using just-in-time provisioning instead of long-lived, statically provisioned accounts
By issuing every vendor a permanent directory account on day one
By requiring vendors to share a single generic account
By outsourcing identity management to the vendor's own IT department
why: Just-in-time provisioning creates the vendor's identity and access at the point it's needed and removes it when it's no longer needed, which matches how vendor engagements actually behave — far better than provisioning a standing account and hoping someone remembers to deprovision it later.
wrong: Permanent accounts and shared generic accounts are exactly the static, poorly-fitting model JIT replaces, and identity management stays under the customer's control rather than being handed to the vendor.

q: What three things does CyberArk Remote Access eliminate the need for?
opts: Firewalls, encryption and network segmentation
VPNs, agents and passwords
Safes, Vaults and policies
Multi-factor authentication, biometrics and QR codes
why: Because identity is proven with biometrics and a dynamic QR code, and the connection is brokered through the cloud service and connector, there is no VPN tunnel to establish, no client agent to install on the vendor's machine, and no password for the vendor to know, share or leak.
wrong: Firewalls and encryption remain part of the underlying architecture rather than being eliminated. Safes, Vaults and policies still control what a user can reach. MFA and biometrics are the replacement mechanism, not something removed.
ref: Remote Access / eliminates VPN, agent, password

q: What is the primary security benefit CyberArk Remote Access delivers?
opts: It mitigates risk by combining Zero Trust and just-in-time access, removing the need for standing passwords and tokens altogether
It encrypts data at rest inside the Vault more strongly than before
It replaces the need for any session recording
It guarantees vendors can never make a mistake during a session
why: By pairing Zero Trust verification with just-in-time provisioning, Remote Access removes the standing credentials — passwords, shared tokens — that are the most common thing attackers steal or vendors mishandle, shrinking the attack surface rather than just monitoring it more closely.
wrong: Vault encryption at rest is unrelated to this benefit and unchanged by Remote Access. Session recording is still very much present, not replaced. No access model can guarantee human error never happens — the benefit is reduced risk, not zero risk.

q: Besides the security improvement, what operational benefit does CyberArk Remote Access provide over conventional VPN or agent-based approaches?
opts: It reduces operational expense and complexity by removing the need to deploy and manage VPNs or agents on third-party machines
It increases the number of administrators required per vendor
It requires a dedicated hardware appliance per vendor site
It lengthens the average onboarding time for a new vendor
why: Because there is nothing to install on the vendor's device and provisioning is just-in-time, the ongoing administrative burden of managing VPN accounts, agent versions and vendor-owned hardware disappears — lowering both cost and operational complexity for the customer's IT team.
wrong: The model reduces administrative effort rather than increasing headcount, needs no per-vendor hardware appliance, and is built specifically to make onboarding faster, not slower.

q: What is the primary function of the CyberArk Mobile App in the Remote Access solution?
opts: To confirm the user's biometric identity and scan the one-time QR code presented at login
To store and manage privileged account passwords
To configure Safes and Vault policies
To host the Remote Access Cloud Service
why: The Mobile App is the endpoint that performs biometric verification (face or fingerprint) and reads the single-use QR code shown during login, tying a real, verified person to that specific authentication attempt.
wrong: Password storage, Safe and policy configuration, and hosting the cloud service are functions of the Vault, PVWA and Remote Access Cloud Service respectively, not the mobile app.

q: Where is a user's biometric data stored when they use the CyberArk Mobile App for Remote Access?
opts: In the Remote Access Cloud Service
On the user's own smartphone — it is never sent to or stored in the cloud service
In the customer's on-premises Vault
On the Remote Access Connector
why: Biometric templates stay local to the device that captured them. The Mobile App performs the match on the phone itself and only communicates the pass or fail result of the QR and biometric challenge outward, so no biometric data is transmitted to or retained by CyberArk's cloud service, the Vault or the Connector.
wrong: The cloud service, the Vault and the Connector all sit outside the phone, and none of them receive or store the biometric template — only the phone does.

q: On what platform is the CyberArk Remote Access Cloud Service deployed?
opts: On-premises at the customer's datacenter
Microsoft Azure, single region
AWS, spread across three Availability Zones
Google Cloud Platform, single zone
why: The Remote Access Cloud Service is a SaaS component hosted on AWS and deployed across three Availability Zones, giving it resilience against a single-AZ failure without requiring the customer to run any of it themselves.
wrong: It is explicitly a cloud, not an on-premises, component, and the hosting platform is AWS rather than Azure or Google Cloud.

q: Which of the following is NOT something the CyberArk Remote Access Cloud Service does?
opts: Lets administrators configure sites, tenants and vendors
Orchestrates communication between the Mobile App, the Connector and the on-premises PAM environment
Stores user biometric data
Runs across three Availability Zones for resilience
why: The Cloud Service is the orchestration and administration layer — it's where sites, tenants and vendors get configured and where the Mobile App, Connector and PAM environment are coordinated — but by design it never receives or stores biometric data, which stays on the user's phone.
wrong: Site, tenant and vendor configuration, orchestration between components, and multi-AZ deployment are all genuine, documented functions of the Cloud Service — only biometric storage is excluded from it.

q: What is the role of the Remote Access Connector?
opts: It brokers connections between the Remote Access Cloud Service and the customer's on-premises PAM environment
It stores vendor passwords locally for offline use
It replaces the PVWA as the web login portal
It performs biometric matching in place of the Mobile App
why: The Connector is the bridge component: deployed on the customer side, it brokers the connection between the cloud-hosted Remote Access service and the on-premises (or Privilege Cloud) PAM environment, so the customer never has to expose the Vault directly to the internet.
wrong: The Connector does not store vendor passwords, does not replace the PVWA login portal, and performs no biometric matching — that stays on the phone.

q: Where is the Remote Access Connector installed?
opts: In the Remote Access Cloud Service tenant
On the remote vendor's own laptop
Internally, behind the customer's firewall
On the CyberArk Mobile App
why: The Connector is deployed inside the customer's network, behind the firewall, alongside or near the PAM environment it brokers access to. This keeps the customer's secrets and internal network topology under their own control rather than exposed to the cloud.
wrong: It is not part of the cloud tenant, it is never installed on a vendor's personal device, and it is a separate server-side component from the Mobile App entirely.

q: What does the HTML5 Gateway do in the Remote Access architecture?
opts: It translates the incoming web protocol into outgoing RDP over TLS, tunneling the session between the Connector and the PSM
It performs the initial biometric authentication check
It stores the Vault's encryption keys
It issues the one-time QR codes shown at login
why: Because the end user connects through a browser, something has to convert that web session into the RDP-over-TLS traffic the target and the PSM actually speak. That is the HTML5 Gateway's job — it tunnels the session between the Connector and the Privileged Session Manager.
wrong: Biometric authentication happens on the phone, encryption keys belong to the Vault and Connector, and QR codes are generated by the Remote Access service — none of those is the Gateway's function.

q: Is the HTML5 Gateway deployed only in the cloud?
opts: Yes, it exists solely as part of the Remote Access Cloud Service
No, it is deployed on-premises, internally alongside the other customer-side components
Yes, but only for customers on the Enterprise tier
No, it is bundled entirely inside the CyberArk Mobile App
why: Like the Connector, the HTML5 Gateway is installed inside the customer's environment. It has to be, since its job is tunneling traffic onward to the on-premises PSM — a cloud-only component couldn't reach an internal target.
wrong: There is no cloud-only or tier-gated version of the Gateway, and it is a server-side component entirely separate from the Mobile App.

q: What role does the customer's CyberArk PAM solution play in the Remote Access architecture?
opts: It provides visibility and control of remote privileged activity — sessions are still brokered through the PSM and automatically recorded and monitored
It only stores the biometric templates used for authentication
It functions purely as a backup path if the Cloud Service is down
It issues the vendor's one-time QR codes
why: Remote Access handles who the user is and whether they should get in; PAM still handles what happens once they're connected. Because the session is brokered through the PSM exactly as an internal privileged session would be, it is automatically isolated, recorded and monitored — giving the customer the same visibility and control over remote activity as over local activity.
wrong: Biometric templates never leave the phone, PAM is not a failover path for the Cloud Service, and QR codes come from the Remote Access service, not PAM.

q: What is the purpose of the Traffic Managers in the Remote Access infrastructure?
opts: To support encrypted sessions from the remote user's endpoint to the nearest PVWA and HTML5 Gateway, minimizing latency
To manage vendor invitation emails
To enforce password complexity rules
To back up the Vault database
why: Traffic Managers route the remote user's encrypted session to the closest available PVWA and HTML5 Gateway, keeping the network path short and latency low regardless of where in the world the user happens to be connecting from.
wrong: Invitation emails, password policy and Vault backups are all handled by other parts of the platform — the Traffic Managers exist purely to optimize the routing of live session traffic.

q: How does a remote user authenticate to the CyberArk web portal (PVWA) using Remote Access?
opts: They enter a password that is checked against Active Directory
They log in to the PVWA, which displays a one-time, short-lived QR code; scanning it with the CyberArk Mobile App and passing a biometric check grants access
They call a help desk to have an administrator unlock the session manually
They insert a smart card issued by CyberArk
why: The PVWA displays a QR code that is unique to that login attempt and expires quickly. The user scans it with the Mobile App, which also performs the biometric check (face or fingerprint); only when both the QR code and the biometric pass does the portal grant access.
wrong: No password is checked against a directory in this flow, no help desk step is involved, and no physical smart card is issued — the whole point of the design is to avoid exactly those older mechanisms.

q: In the Remote Access connection flow, what happens once the user's authentication reaches the Remote Access Connector?
opts: The initial encryption tunnel from the browser ends there, and the Connector opens a new encrypted channel directly to the PVWA
The session is immediately terminated for security review
A new tunnel is opened back out to the Remote Access Cloud Service
The user is redirected to re-authenticate from scratch
why: The Connector is a genuine broker, not just a relay: the browser's original encrypted tunnel ends at the Connector, and a fresh encrypted channel is then opened directly to the PVWA to carry the rest of the session. The cloud service is not part of this second leg at all.
wrong: The session is not terminated at this point — this is the middle of establishing access, not a failure. The new channel goes inward to the PVWA, not back out to the cloud, and no separate re-authentication step is triggered here.

q: What does the Remote Access Connector validate before opening the new encrypted channel to the PVWA?
opts: The user's IP geolocation only
The session and user cookies, along with the PVWA and HTML5 Gateway certificates
The vendor's invoice and contract status
The Mobile App's battery level
why: Before extending trust into the internal network, the Connector checks the session cookie, the user cookie, and the certificates presented by the PVWA and the HTML5 Gateway — confirming both who the session belongs to and that it is talking to genuine, expected internal endpoints.
wrong: Geolocation alone would be a weak check and isn't what's validated here, and contract status or device battery level are not security controls the Connector evaluates at all.

q: Once a remote user's identity has been verified, what determines which privileged accounts the Remote Access Connector grants them access to?
opts: The vendor's invoice amount
Their existing Safe permissions in the Vault
A random selection made by the Cloud Service
Whatever account the vendor last used, regardless of current permissions
why: Verifying identity only answers who the user is. What they can actually reach is still governed the same way it always is in PAM — by the Safe permissions assigned to their Vault user, directly or through group and directory-mapping membership.
wrong: Invoicing has no bearing on access control, access is never randomly assigned, and past usage doesn't override current permission checks — every connection is evaluated against the user's current Safe permissions.

q: What technology allows a Remote Access session to remain browser-agnostic and isolated from the end user's device?
opts: A dedicated Flash plug-in installed in the browser
End-to-end encryption of the session, brokered through the PSM rather than run natively on the endpoint
A locally cached copy of the target password
A proprietary browser that must be installed by the vendor
why: Because the session is end-to-end encrypted and brokered through the infrastructure rather than executed as a native client on the user's own machine, it doesn't matter which standard browser the user has — the session runs isolated from, and independent of, whatever is on the endpoint.
wrong: There is no Flash dependency, no cached password sitting on the endpoint, and no special browser to install — isolation comes from how the session is brokered, not from browser-specific software.

q: What is the benefit of monitoring privileged access activity in real time through Remote Access's isolated sessions?
opts: It decreases the accuracy of compliance audits
It helps detect in-progress attacks and supports compliance audits with a full record of activity
It prevents any session from ever being recorded, for privacy
It has no measurable security benefit
why: Because every remote privileged session is brokered through the PSM like any other privileged session, it is recorded and can be watched live — giving security teams a chance to catch an attack while it's happening rather than only after the fact, while also producing the audit trail compliance frameworks require.
wrong: Monitoring improves, rather than undermines, compliance accuracy, sessions are recorded rather than exempted from recording, and the security value of catching live attacks is the opposite of no benefit.

q: When a customer signs up for a Remote Access tenant hosted in a particular CyberArk datacenter, what happens to that tenant's data?
opts: It is automatically replicated to every other CyberArk datacenter
It is stored only in that specific datacenter
It is copied to the customer's own on-premises backup nightly
It is distributed randomly across whichever datacenter has spare capacity
why: A tenant is provisioned in a specific datacenter, and its data stays there rather than being replicated globally — a data-residency model that matters for customers with regulatory or contractual requirements about where their data physically lives.
wrong: There is no automatic cross-datacenter replication, no automatic nightly export to customer-owned storage, and no random distribution — the tenant's home datacenter is fixed at provisioning time.

q: Which operating systems can the Remote Access Connector be deployed on?
opts: Windows and macOS
Ubuntu and Red Hat
CentOS and Debian only
Solaris and AIX
why: The Connector ships for Ubuntu and Red Hat Linux, matching the Docker-based deployment model it uses — administrators pick either distribution for the on-premises host that will run the Connector container.
wrong: The Connector is a Linux-only component, so Windows and macOS are not supported hosts. CentOS/Debian and Solaris/AIX are not the documented supported platforms.

q: What technology is the Remote Access Connector built on to simplify its management and deployment?
opts: A Docker container
A Kubernetes cluster the customer must manage
A Windows Service
A browser extension
why: Packaging the Connector as a Docker container means deployment, updates and management follow a simple, consistent container lifecycle rather than requiring a bespoke installer or a full orchestration platform.
wrong: It doesn't require the customer to stand up Kubernetes, it isn't a Windows Service since the Connector runs on Linux, and it is a server-side component, not a browser extension.

q: Which outbound port does the Remote Access Connector use to communicate with the Remote Access Cloud Service?
opts: Port 80
Port 22
Port 443
Port 8080
why: The Connector reaches out to the Cloud Service over standard outbound HTTPS, port 443 — a port already open on almost every corporate firewall for web traffic, which is part of why the Connector needs no special inbound firewall rules.
wrong: Port 80 is unencrypted HTTP, port 22 is SSH, and port 8080 is a common alternate web port — none of these is the port the Connector actually uses for this outbound connection.

q: How does Remote Access achieve high availability and load balancing at a given customer site?
opts: By supporting multiple Connectors deployed for that site
By deploying a single, oversized Connector instance
By failing over to the Remote Access Cloud Service itself
By routing all traffic through the HTML5 Gateway alone
why: A site can run more than one Connector. With multiple Connectors online, load is spread across them and the loss of any single Connector doesn't take the site's Remote Access connectivity down with it.
wrong: A single larger instance would still be a single point of failure, the Cloud Service does not substitute for an on-premises broker, and the Gateway alone does not provide Connector redundancy.

q: Where can an administrator see how many Connectors are installed for each site?
opts: On the Sites page, where clicking the connector count opens detailed information about each Connector
In the CyberArk Mobile App
In the Vault's PrivateArk Client
In the vendor invitation email
why: The Sites page lists each site along with its connector count; clicking that number drills into the per-Connector detail — version, connectivity, LDAP status and more — covered on the Connectors page.
wrong: The Mobile App is an end-user tool with no site administration view, the PrivateArk Client manages the Vault rather than Remote Access sites, and invitation emails carry no infrastructure information.

q: Which of the following is NOT information displayed on the Connectors page for a site?
opts: The Connector's software version
Whether the Connector is connected to the SaaS service
The number of failed authentication attempts
Whether the LDAP service is running on the Connector
why: The Connectors page is an infrastructure health view: version, SaaS connectivity status, LDAP service status, and the number of users and applications supported through that Connector. Failed authentication attempts are an audit or security detail, not something surfaced on this operational page.
wrong: Version, SaaS connection status and LDAP service status are all genuinely shown on the Connectors page — only the failed-authentication count is missing from it.

q: Which service running on the Remote Access Connector is required to use the Just-in-Time Vendor and Group feature?
opts: The Kerberos service
The LDAP service
The SAML service
The RADIUS service
why: The Connector runs a local LDAP service, VendorLDAP, that the Just-in-Time Vendor and Group feature depends on to create and manage vendor users and groups on demand. If that LDAP service isn't running, JIT provisioning through the Connector doesn't work.
wrong: Kerberos, SAML and RADIUS are authentication protocols the Connector does not rely on for this specific feature — it is specifically the LDAP service that JIT Vendor and Group provisioning needs.

q: What does the Just-in-Time Vendor and Group feature do?
opts: It provisions users into the Vault directly from the Connector, on demand, rather than requiring accounts to be pre-created
It stores vendor passwords for later reuse
It configures the customer's outbound firewall rules
It schedules automatic Vault backups
why: Instead of an administrator pre-creating Vault users for every vendor, this feature provisions the Vault user, its group membership and therefore its Safe access on demand, at the point the vendor actually needs it — the mechanical heart of just-in-time access for Remote Access.
wrong: No vendor password is stored for reuse, since the model avoids vendor-managed passwords entirely, and firewall configuration and Vault backup scheduling are unrelated administrative tasks.

q: What does the `Connector.log` file contain?
opts: Only failed login attempts
The general status of the Connector, including status messages related to other components it interacts with
Network latency measurements only
A list of installed applications
why: `Connector.log` is the Connector's own general status log — the first place to look for what the Connector itself is doing, plus status information touching the other pieces (Cloud Service, PVWA, Gateway) it talks to.
wrong: It is not limited to failed logins, it isn't a latency-only measurement log, and it doesn't function as an application inventory — those are narrower purposes than what this log actually records.

q: Which log file contains the proxy log of user sessions passing between the Connector, Remote Access SaaS, the PVWA and the HTML5 Gateway?
opts: `Connector.log`
`Nginx-output.log`
OpenLDAP logs
`ssh-client-output.logs`
why: `Nginx-output.log` captures the proxying that happens as a user's session is relayed through the Connector to the SaaS service, the PVWA and the HTML5 Gateway — the log to check when a session in progress seems to be dropping or misrouting.
wrong: `Connector.log` is the broader component-status log, the OpenLDAP logs cover directory and JIT activity, and `ssh-client-output.logs` covers the secure tunnel to the SaaS service specifically — none of those is the session proxy log.

q: What kind of information do the OpenLDAP logs on the Connector contain?
opts: Web application firewall events
Just-in-Time functionality logs, including user and group creation and VendorLDAP activity
Network latency to the nearest Traffic Manager
PVWA certificate renewal events
why: Because VendorLDAP is the local directory the JIT Vendor and Group feature relies on, the OpenLDAP logs are where that activity shows up — user and group creation events and general VendorLDAP behavior.
wrong: There is no WAF component logging here, latency to Traffic Managers is not what this directory service logs, and certificate renewal is unrelated to LDAP directory activity.

q: Which log file records connectivity to the Remote Access SaaS service, including information about the secure tunnel?
opts: `Connector.log`
OpenLDAP logs
`ssh-client-output.logs`
`Nginx-output.log`
why: `ssh-client-output.logs` is specifically about the outbound secure tunnel the Connector maintains to the Remote Access SaaS service — the log to check when a Connector shows as disconnected from the cloud.
wrong: `Connector.log` is the general component-status log, the OpenLDAP logs cover directory and JIT activity, and `Nginx-output.log` covers session proxying rather than the SaaS tunnel itself.

q: Which command gathers Remote Access Connector logs automatically and bundles them into a `.tar.gz` file?
opts: `bundle-logs`
`create-logs`
`generate-logs`
`get-logs`
why: `get-logs` is the built-in command that collects the relevant Connector log files for you and packages them into a single `.tar.gz` archive, which is far faster than hunting down each log manually when opening a support case.
wrong: `bundle-logs`, `create-logs` and `generate-logs` are not the documented command — only `get-logs` performs this automated collection.
ref: Remote Access Connector logs / get-logs command

q: Where is the Remote Access Connector's log data located on disk for manual collection?
opts: `/home/<user>/remote-logs/`
`/opt/remote-connector-logs/`
`/var/lib/docker/volumes/remote-access.logs/_data/`
`/usr/local/logs/connector`
why: Because the Connector runs inside a Docker container, its persistent log data lives in the corresponding Docker volume on the host, at `/var/lib/docker/volumes/remote-access.logs/_data/`.
wrong: None of the other paths is the documented location — the log data specifically lives under the Docker volume backing the Connector container, not in a standalone application directory.
ref: Remote Access Connector logs / manual log path

q: Where is the Remote Access CLI log file located?
opts: `/opt/remote-access-cli/logs/`
`/home/<user>/snap/remote-access-cli/common/logs/connector-cli.log`
`/var/lib/docker/cli-logs/_data/`
`/usr/snap/logs/connector-cli`
why: The Remote Access CLI is distributed as a Snap package, so its log lives under the standard Snap common-data path for that package, at `/home/<user>/snap/remote-access-cli/common/logs/connector-cli.log`.
wrong: The other paths don't match the Snap-based install layout the CLI actually uses — this is a Snap application log, not a Docker volume or a generic /opt install.

q: Where is the Remote Access Connector Hardening log file located?
opts: `/var/log/hardening-connector.log`
`/etc/remote-access/hardening-log.txt`
`/opt/remote-access-hardening-log.txt`
`/usr/local/hardening-connector/logs`
why: The Connector's hardening process writes its results to `/opt/remote-access-hardening-log.txt` — useful to check when confirming that OS-level hardening steps applied cleanly during or after Connector installation.
wrong: None of the other paths is the documented hardening log location for the Connector.
ref: Remote Access Connector logs / hardening log

q: Why is the `journalctl` utility required to read log messages processed by `journald`?
opts: Because journald encrypts every log entry
Because journald stores its log data in a binary format rather than plain text
Because journald uploads logs directly to a cloud service
Because journald compresses every entry into `.gz` format on write
why: `journald`, the systemd logging service, stores its data in a binary journal rather than flat text files, so standard text tools like `tail` or `grep` can't read it directly — `journalctl` is the utility built to query and display that binary journal.
wrong: journald does not encrypt entries, does not upload logs to any cloud service, and does not gzip individual entries — the reason for a dedicated utility is purely the binary storage format.

q: Which command shows all logs from a Snap unit such as `snapd`?
opts: `journalctl -u snapd`
`systemctl logs snap`
`snap logs all`
`journalctl -s snap`
why: `journalctl -u <unit>` filters the systemd journal down to a specific unit — `journalctl -u snapd` shows everything logged by the Snap daemon, which is useful since the Remote Access CLI is distributed as a Snap package.
wrong: `systemctl logs`, `snap logs all` and `journalctl -s` are not valid commands for this purpose — `journalctl -u` is the correct, documented syntax for unit-scoped log queries.

q: When an application is provisioned to a vendor or user in Remote Access, what does it give them access to?

The PVWA
The CyberArk Mobile App's settings menu
The customer's Active Directory

q: Where in the Remote Access portal are applications managed?
opts: Under the Security tab
Under the Applications page, within the Site section
Under the Active Directory tab
Under User Management

q: What does the Applications page display for each application?

The application and the number of active sessions connected to it in the last hour
The vendor's full contact details
A list of every Safe in the Vault

q: Which action on an application tile initiates a connection to that application?

Show Configuration

q: What does the **Show configuration** option on an application reveal?

The application-specific authentication information needed to configure Remote Access for that target
A log of every user who has connected
The application's password rotation schedule
why: Show configuration exposes the application-specific settings and authentication details an admin needs when wiring that particular target up for Remote Access — the setup information, not a usage log.
wrong: It isn't an invitation-link history, a connection audit log, or a rotation schedule — it's the configuration detail for the application itself.

q: What is the effect of selecting **Hide** for an application?
opts: It permanently deletes the application from the system
It temporarily deactivates the application, so previously invited vendors can no longer access it, without removing the application itself
It only hides the application from the admin's own view
It revokes the vendor's biometric enrollment
why: Hide is reversible: the application is temporarily deactivated and stops being reachable by invited vendors, but the application record and its configuration remain intact so it can be un-hidden later — unlike Delete, which removes it entirely.
wrong: Deletion is a separate, permanent action; Hide affects vendor access, not just what the admin can see; and it has nothing to do with a vendor's biometric enrollment on their phone.

q: How does deleting an application differ from editing it?
opts: Edit lets you modify the application's settings; Delete removes the application from all screens entirely, which Edit does not do
They are identical actions with different labels
Edit is reversible, Delete only hides the application temporarily
Delete only removes the application for a single vendor
why: Edit changes the application's configuration while keeping it in place. Delete is destructive at the application level — it removes the application from every screen in the portal, not just from one vendor's view or session.

q: What must a company user do before they can connect to applications through Remote Access?
opts: Purchase an additional Remote Access license
Authenticate to Remote Access using their Active Directory credentials
Download a VPN client
Wait 24 hours after account creation

q: Where does a company user set their Active Directory credentials in the CyberArk Mobile App?

In the application-specific settings for each target
Under the credentials button in the app's menu
In the Remote Access web portal only, never in the app

Their account is automatically elevated to tenant admin
Their biometric enrollment is deleted and must be redone

q: What do you select in the Remote Access portal to connect to the PVWA?
opts: Applications
Active Directory
User Management
Vendor Invitation

wrong: Active Directory, User Management and Vendor Invitation are administrative or configuration areas, not the place from which an ordinary user launches a connection.

q: After connecting to the PVWA through Remote Access, which username is used to log in to the application?
opts: The CyberArk Mobile App username
The tenant admin's username
The user's Active Directory username
The invited vendor's display name

wrong: There is no separate Mobile App username, the tenant admin's identity is not substituted for the connecting user's, and a display name is cosmetic, not a login credential.

q: Which of the following can CyberArk Remote Access be integrated with? (Choose three)
opts: Active Directory
CyberArk Identity
An external Identity Provider
A generic on-premises RADIUS server

q: Before a company user can be invited to Remote Access, what must they already have done?

Downloaded the CyberArk Mobile app and registered for Remote Access

q: Where does a tenant admin go in the Remote Access portal to invite company users?
opts: Identities > Users
Applications > Add

q: Which two methods can an admin use to invite a new company user to Remote Access?

Only a physical letter with a printed activation code
Automatic invitation with no admin action required

q: Where do tenant admins manage company users, and what action can they take on an individual user there?
opts: In the Users pane, where they can activate or deactivate a user
In the Applications tab, where they can rename a user
In the Sites page, where they can only view a user's IP address
In the Security settings, where they can reset a user's biometric enrollment remotely

wrong: Renaming users isn't done from the Applications tab, the Sites page doesn't expose user IP addresses, and biometric enrollment is device-local and isn't something an admin resets remotely from Security settings.

q: What privilege does a company user gain when they are elevated to tenant admin?
opts: The ability to manage Remote Access applications and invite vendors
Read-only visibility into the Vault's audit log, nothing more
The ability to invite vendors, but not to manage applications
No additional privilege beyond a standard company user

q: What is the purpose of the Vendor Manager role in Remote Access?

It disables a company user's ability to log in

The timeframe they can grant on invitations

q: What does the **allow this vendor to invite other vendors** setting do?

It converts the vendor into a tenant admin
It disables that vendor's own access to applications

wrong: It does not scan or invite an address book automatically, it does not grant tenant admin rights, and it has no effect on the inviting vendor's own application access.

q: Who is permitted to invite a vendor to join Remote Access?

A tenant admin, a company user with Vendor Manager permissions, or a vendor delegated that permission
Only CyberArk support
Any user, with no permission required

q: What is the main rationale behind letting tenant admins delegate Vendor Manager permissions rather than inviting every vendor themselves?

It is required because tenant admins are technically incapable of sending invitations
It removes the need for any auditing of vendor invitations
It guarantees vendors never need to be deactivated

q: What does integrating CyberArk Identity with Remote Access provide?

A replacement for the CyberArk Mobile App's biometric check

Backing up and restoring user data

q: Which of the following are configurable fields on the vendor invitation form? (Choose four)

Automatic only applies to company users; manual only applies to vendors

q: Where is self-service vendor registration enabled in Remote Access?

Under Sites > Applications
In the CyberArk Mobile App settings
In the Vault's PrivateArk Client

q: How does the self-service vendor flow let a vendor request access without first receiving a direct invitation?

Self-service is only available to internal company users, not external vendors

q: What can an admin do with a vendor's self-service access request?

Nothing — self-service requests bypass admin review entirely
Forward it to CyberArk support for a decision

q: When an admin clicks **confirm and invite** on a pending self-service vendor request, what happens?

opts: Delete removes both the Vault user and the VendorLDAP user immediately, with no 24-hour delay
Delete only removes the VendorLDAP user, exactly like deactivation
Delete is reversible, deactivation is not
Delete only affects the vendor's biometric enrollment
why: Delete is the more immediate, more final action: both the Vault user and the VendorLDAP user are removed right away, unlike deactivation, where VendorLDAP removal happens first and the Vault user follows roughly a day later.
wrong: Delete's effect on the Vault user is exactly what sets it apart from deactivation, not something it shares with it. Reversibility runs the other way in practice, and the action targets the accounts, not just phone-side biometric data.

q: If a vendor's access timeframe has expired, what can an admin do without re-inviting them from scratch?
opts: Extend the vendor's access timeframe directly
Nothing — the vendor must always be re-invited after expiration
Only CyberArk support can extend an expired timeframe
Restore access automatically after 30 days with no admin action
why: An admin can simply extend an already-expired vendor's access timeframe, picking up where the original engagement left off, rather than tearing down and rebuilding the whole invitation and registration process.
wrong: Re-invitation is not the only path — extension exists precisely to avoid it. This is a customer-admin action, not something requiring CyberArk support, and nothing restores automatically without deliberate admin action.
ref: Remote Access / extending expired vendor access

q: Where is the setting for automatically removing expired vendors located, and what is its minimum interval?
opts: Under Settings > Identities, with a minimum interval of 30 days
Under Sites > Connectors, with a minimum interval of 24 hours
Under Applications > Configuration, with no minimum interval
Under Identities > Vendors, with a minimum interval of 7 days
why: The auto-remove-after-expiration control lives under Settings > Identities, and it can't be set to trigger sooner than 30 days after a vendor's timeframe expires — a floor that prevents overly aggressive automatic cleanup.
wrong: Connectors and Applications configuration areas don't host this setting, and 24 hours or 7 days both undercut the documented 30-day minimum interval.

q: How is a new vendor sign-up confirmed as part of the registration process?
opts: Via a push notification that the vendor confirms through the CyberArk Mobile App or the web portal
By the vendor mailing a signed paper form to the tenant admin
Automatically, with no confirmation step at all
Only by a phone call placed to CyberArk support
why: Completing sign-up triggers a push notification that the vendor confirms either in the Mobile App or through the portal, a lightweight, real-time confirmation step consistent with the rest of the mobile-first registration flow.
wrong: There's no paper-based confirmation step, sign-up isn't confirmed with zero human involvement, and CyberArk support has no role in confirming an individual vendor's registration.

q: If a company user is deleted from the Users list in Remote Access, can they be brought back?
opts: No, once deleted a person can never be invited again under any circumstance
Yes — they can be invited again at any time
Only if CyberArk support manually restores them
Only after a mandatory 90-day waiting period
why: Deletion removes the current account, but it doesn't blacklist the person — an admin can simply issue them a fresh invitation whenever needed, and they go through registration again like any new invitee.
wrong: There's no permanent lockout, no CyberArk-support-only restore process, and no fixed waiting period before someone can be re-invited.
ref: Remote Access / re-inviting a deleted user

q: Which of the following is NOT a method of inviting a vendor to join Remote Access?
opts: Sending an email invitation
Generating a QR code
Assigning the vendor directly to a Safe
Sending an SMS token invitation
why: Email, QR code and SMS token are all genuine ways to deliver a vendor invitation. Assigning Safe access is a downstream authorization step that happens after a vendor identity exists — it is not itself a way of inviting someone.
wrong: Email, QR code and SMS are each documented invitation delivery methods — Safe assignment is a permissions action, not an invitation mechanism.

q: What is Secure Native Access?
opts: A browser-only HTML5 replacement for RDP
VPN-less, password-less native RDP access to targets, available for Windows and Mac desktop clients and Android mobile
A hardware token required for every RDP session
A feature limited to Linux SSH sessions only
why: Secure Native Access extends VPN-less, password-less access beyond the browser: it lets users connect with a genuine native RDP session from Windows or Mac desktop clients, or from an Android mobile device, rather than being limited to the HTML5 in-browser experience.
wrong: It is specifically a native-client capability, not a browser-only HTML5 feature, it needs no hardware token, and it is an RDP-focused capability rather than an SSH one.

q: When using Secure Native Access, which RDP client must a user use?
opts: A proprietary CyberArk-branded RDP client only
Whichever RDP client the user prefers — they are free to use their own client of choice
Microsoft Remote Desktop only, with no alternatives permitted
No client is used; the connection is entirely browser-based
why: Secure Native Access is built to work with whatever native RDP client the user already prefers, rather than forcing a proprietary client — the security controls travel with the connection rather than being baked into a specific piece of client software.
wrong: There's no mandated proprietary client, no restriction to Microsoft's client specifically, and this is explicitly a native-client feature, not a browser-based one.

q: What is the minimum Remote Access Connector version required to support Secure Native Access?
why: Secure Native Access depends on connector-side capabilities that were introduced starting with Connector version `1.0.12002` — sites running an older connector need to upgrade before the feature becomes available.
wrong: The other version numbers do not correspond to the documented minimum required for this feature.
ref: Secure Native Access / minimum connector version

q: Which of the following are prerequisites for a user to use Secure Native Access? (Choose three)
opts: The user has access to the target application or account
The user is registered to the CyberArk Mobile App
The user is authenticated to their company directory
The connector is running in an isolated network segment with no internet access
why: Three things have to be true before Secure Native Access will work for a user: they need existing access to the target, they need to be registered to the Mobile App, which handles the push and biometric approval, and they need to be authenticated to their company directory.
wrong: Network isolation for the connector is not a prerequisite — the connector specifically needs outbound reachability to the Remote Access Cloud Service, the opposite of being air-gapped.

q: Who enables Secure Native Access for a given application, and where?
opts: A tenant admin, under Sites > Applications, by configuring an external URL prefix
Any company user, from their own profile settings
Automatically, for every application, with no configuration needed
CyberArk support, via a backend ticket
why: Secure Native Access is turned on per application rather than tenant-wide. A tenant admin enables it under Sites > Applications and configures the external URL prefix the native client will use to reach that target.
wrong: Ordinary company users have no ability to enable this themselves, it is not on by default for every application, and it is a self-service admin configuration step, not something requiring a CyberArk support ticket.
ref: Secure Native Access / enabling per application

q: What are the two ways a user can connect using Secure Native Access?
opts: Download a pre-configured RDP file, or manually configure a new RDP target using properties supplied by the portal
Only by calling the help desk for a session code
Only through a browser-embedded RDP viewer
Only by installing a dedicated CyberArk client agent
why: A user can either download an RDP file the portal has already configured for them and open it directly, or manually build a new RDP connection profile using the connection properties the portal supplies — two paths to the same native session.
wrong: There is no help-desk-issued session code, no browser-embedded viewer involved since that's the HTML5 path rather than this one, and no separate CyberArk client agent to install.

q: What must a user confirm on their mobile device to approve a Secure Native Access connection?
opts: A mobile push notification confirming the request originated from the same machine that triggered the session, approved with Face ID or Touch ID
Nothing — the connection opens automatically with no approval step
A typed six-digit code read from the RDP client
A phone call from an automated verification system
why: The mobile app pushes an approval request tied specifically to the machine that initiated the RDP session, and the user confirms it biometrically with Face ID or Touch ID, binding the approval to both the right person and the right device, which blocks a relayed or phished request from a different machine.
wrong: Approval is required, not automatic; there's no typed numeric code involved in this step; and no automated phone call is part of the flow.
ref: Secure Native Access / push and biometric approval

q: What optional prompt can be configured as part of a Secure Native Access connection request?
opts: A reason-for-access prompt the user must answer before connecting
A request for the user's home address
A CAPTCHA challenge
A request to upload a photo ID
why: Admins can optionally require the user to supply a reason for access before the connection completes — useful context captured at the moment of connection, particularly for audit and compliance purposes.
wrong: Home address, CAPTCHA and photo ID uploads are not part of this workflow — the optional prompt specifically captures a stated reason for the access request.
ref: Secure Native Access / reason for access prompt

q: How is a Secure Native Access RDP connection protected, even though it uses the user's own native client?
opts: It is end-to-end encrypted and brokered directly to the target, with the PSM still protecting and isolating the session
It relies solely on the operating system's built-in RDP encryption with no additional CyberArk protection
It is unprotected, since native clients bypass PSM entirely
It uses the same biometric check as the browser flow instead of session-level protection
why: Using a native client changes how the user connects, not what protects the session. The connection is still end-to-end encrypted and brokered to the target, and the PSM still isolates and protects it — the credential is never exposed directly to the user's native client.
wrong: CyberArk's controls add to, rather than replace, the OS's own RDP encryption, and native clients specifically do not bypass PSM, which would defeat the point of the feature. Biometrics authorize the request; they are not what protects the live session.

q: If a target account is protected by Dual Control, does Secure Native Access bypass the approval requirement?
opts: No — Dual Control-protected accounts still require approval even when accessed via Secure Native Access
Yes, native RDP connections automatically bypass Dual Control
Only during business hours does Dual Control still apply
Dual Control is disabled automatically the first time Secure Native Access is enabled
why: Secure Native Access is a connection method, not an override of PAM's access controls — an account still under Dual Control continues to require that approval regardless of whether the session comes in through the browser or a native client.
wrong: There is no bypass for native connections, no time-of-day exception, and enabling Secure Native Access has no side effect of disabling Dual Control on any account.
ref: Secure Native Access / Dual Control still enforced

q: What does the offline access feature allow when the Remote Access or PAM service is unavailable?
opts: The Mobile App can show a cached password stored on the device
The user is automatically granted a temporary generic password
All active sessions are automatically extended indefinitely
The Connector switches to a local backup Vault
why: Offline access lets the Mobile App present a previously cached password so a user isn't completely locked out during a genuine service outage — a deliberate, controlled exception rather than a general bypass of normal retrieval.
wrong: No generic temporary password is issued, session extension isn't the mechanism here, and there is no local backup Vault the Connector fails over to.

q: On which platforms is offline access available, and what does it require?
opts: All Privilege Cloud versions and self-hosted PAM 10.3+, and it requires company-directory authentication
Only Privilege Cloud, and it requires no authentication at all
Only self-hosted PAM versions below 10.3
Only Android devices, regardless of PAM version
why: Offline access is broadly available across every Privilege Cloud version, plus self-hosted PAM from 10.3 onward, but it still requires the user to be authenticated to their company directory — caching a password offline doesn't remove that baseline identity check.
wrong: It is not Privilege-Cloud-only, self-hosted support starts at 10.3 rather than being limited to versions before it, and it isn't restricted to a single mobile platform.
ref: Secure Native Access / offline access availability

q: How is offline access controlled for company users versus vendors?
opts: There is a single toggle that applies identically to both populations
There are separate admin toggles — one for company users and one for vendors — controlled independently
Vendors can never be granted offline access under any configuration
Company users can never be granted offline access under any configuration
why: An admin can enable offline access for company users without enabling it for vendors, or vice versa, because the two populations have independent toggles, letting the organization apply a tighter policy to external vendors if it chooses.
wrong: The controls are not combined into a single switch, and neither population is unconditionally barred from offline access — availability is a configurable admin choice for each group.
ref: Secure Native Access / offline access toggles

q: What two additional controls exist for offline access beyond the basic on and off toggles?
opts: A configurable reminder to re-sync the cached password per the rotation policy, and an unrestricted mode that allows offline viewing regardless of service availability
A mandatory 5-minute session timeout and a ban on all password copying
A requirement to re-register biometrics weekly and a ban on Android devices
A hard cap of one offline view per account, ever
why: Beyond simply turning the feature on, admins can configure a reminder that nudges users to re-sync their cached password in step with the account's rotation policy, and can enable an unrestricted mode that lets users view the cached password anytime, not only during an actual outage.
wrong: There's no mandatory 5-minute timeout or blanket copy-paste ban tied to this feature, no weekly biometric re-registration requirement or Android ban, and no fixed one-time-ever viewing cap.
ref: Secure Native Access / offline access controls

q: Which types of accounts cannot be saved for offline access? (Choose two)
opts: Accounts under enforced check-in/check-out exclusive access
Accounts under a one-time-password policy
Accounts with a long, complex password
Accounts managed by the CPM under normal rotation
why: Offline caching a password would undermine both of these controls: exclusive check-in/check-out access is meant to guarantee only one person holds the password at a time, and a one-time-password policy assumes the password is invalidated after a single use — neither survives being cached indefinitely on a phone.
wrong: Password length and complexity, and ordinary CPM-managed rotation, don't conflict with offline caching — an account can be perfectly normal in those respects and still be eligible for offline access.
ref: Secure Native Access / offline access exclusions

q: What does the tenant admin's Activities pane provide?
opts: Time-range and activity-type filters, with expandable rows for further detail on each logged activity
A live video feed of every session, with no filtering
A single unfiltered list of every event since tenant creation
Only a count of total logins, with no other detail
why: The Activities pane is a filterable audit view: an admin narrows results by time range and activity type, then expands individual rows to see more detail about a specific logged event.
wrong: It is not a live video feed, since that is session recording through PAM, a different feature, and it is filterable rather than a single flat, unfiltered list or a bare login counter.

q: Where can a user view the Remote Access license, and what does that view show?
opts: From the user's profile dropdown, showing subscriptions in use, sessions, expiration date, and a breakdown by users and vendors
From the Applications page, showing only the number of applications configured
From the Sites page, showing only connector counts
Licensing information is not visible in the portal at all
why: The license summary is reachable from the profile dropdown and gives a consolidated picture: subscriptions consumed, session counts, the expiration date, and how consumption splits between company users and vendors.
wrong: The Applications and Sites pages surface different, unrelated information, and license visibility is very much available in the portal, not hidden from it.

q: At what license consumption levels does Remote Access show warning indicators, and what do they look like?
opts: An orange warning triangle at 90% consumed, and a red warning at 100% consumed
A yellow banner at 50% and a red banner at 75%
No visual warning is ever shown regardless of consumption
A single red warning that appears only after the license has expired
why: The license view escalates visually as consumption climbs: an orange warning triangle appears once usage hits 90%, and it turns red at full, 100% consumption, giving admins advance notice before they actually run out.
wrong: The thresholds are 90% and 100%, not 50%/75%, a warning is shown well before full consumption rather than never, and the warning appears at high consumption, not only after outright expiration.

q: How does a Remote Access user consume licenses, and what is the exception?
opts: Every Remote Access user consumes a Remote Access license, and also a Vault license once a corresponding Vault user exists for them, except while their status is Deactivated
Every user consumes two Remote Access licenses and no Vault license, with no exceptions
Only vendors consume any license; company users are free
License consumption is fixed at tenant creation and never changes per user
why: Two license pools are in play: the Remote Access license every user consumes just by existing, and a Vault license consumed once that user actually has a corresponding Vault account. The one exception is a Deactivated user, who does not draw a Vault license while in that status.
wrong: Consumption is one Remote Access license per user, not two, and there is a genuine Vault-license dimension, so it isn't Remote-Access-only. Company users consume licenses exactly like vendors do, and consumption changes as users are added, deactivated or deleted — it isn't fixed at creation.

q: What happens immediately when a Remote Access account is created?
opts: Matching VendorLDAP and Vault users are created for that account at the same time
Only a Remote Access record is created; VendorLDAP and Vault users are created weeks later
A Vault user is created, but no VendorLDAP entry is ever made
Nothing else happens until the user's first login
why: Account creation immediately provisions the full chain — the Remote Access account, its VendorLDAP entry, and its Vault user are all created together, rather than being staggered or deferred to first login.
wrong: There is no multi-week delay, VendorLDAP provisioning is very much part of the flow rather than skipped, and the dependent objects are created at creation time, not deferred until the user first logs in.

q: What happens to a user invited for a fixed access timeframe if that timeframe is not extended?
opts: They are auto-deactivated 24 hours after the timeframe expires
They are deleted instantly the moment the timeframe ends, with no delay
They remain fully active indefinitely unless an admin manually intervenes
Their access is automatically extended by another full timeframe
why: Expiration isn't instantaneous in its effect — there's a 24-hour grace period after the timeframe ends before the user is automatically deactivated, after which the standard deactivation cascade of VendorLDAP removal now and Vault removal roughly a day later applies.
wrong: There is a defined 24-hour delay rather than an instant deletion, the account does not stay active forever without intervention, and expiration does not silently auto-renew the access window.

q: How does an administrator verify that vendors are consuming the correct license type, and how is a mismatch corrected?
opts: Run a license-capacity report from the PrivateArk Client to confirm vendors consume the External User license type rather than an EPV license, then fix mismatches via the Directory Mapping User Template or by deleting stray vendor users directly from the Vault
Check the Mobile App's settings screen, and fix mismatches by reinstalling the Connector
There is no way to verify license type consumption
Run a report from the HTML5 Gateway, and fix mismatches by rotating all vendor passwords
why: The PrivateArk Client's license-capacity report shows which license type each Vault user is actually drawing from, confirming vendors land on the External User license rather than consuming an Enterprise Password Vault (EPV) license. Where that's wrong, the fix is either correcting the Directory Mapping User Template so future vendors provision correctly, or manually deleting stray vendor users created under the wrong template.
wrong: The Mobile App has no license-capacity reporting function, and reinstalling the Connector or rotating passwords does nothing to fix a license-type misassignment — verification is a Vault-side concern handled through the PrivateArk Client, not the Gateway.

q: Where do tenant admins manage vendor accounts in the Remote Access portal?
opts: In the Vendors list, functioning as the vendor-side counterpart to the company Users pane
In the Applications page, mixed in with application tiles
In the Sites page, listed alongside connectors
In the CyberArk Mobile App's admin panel
why: Vendors get their own dedicated list in the portal, the Vendors list, mirroring the Users pane used for company users, and it's where an admin activates, deactivates, deletes or extends the timeframe of individual vendor accounts.
wrong: Vendors aren't mixed into the Applications page or the Sites and Connectors view, and there is no admin panel inside the end-user-facing Mobile App — vendor administration is a portal-side function.
